name: Knee On Belly Control
keyCorrections: If you keep getting swept: your weight is too far forward — sit back slightly and keep your hips under you
If they trap your foot: pummel your foot free immediately by circling it toward your body
If they escape before you can react: you stayed too long — commit to a transition earlier
description: Use the knee on the belly and far hip grip to control, transition quickly, and open submissions. Knee-on-belly is the most mobile pin — it sacrifices some control for the ability to transition faster than any other position.
shortInstruction: Drive your knee into their sternum or solar plexus, grip their far hip or collar, and stay ready to transition to mount, side control, or north-south. Do not let them trap your foot.
summary: Knee-on-belly uses your knee as the primary pressure point, creating discomfort that forces the opponent to react, exposing openings for submissions or transitions. The key is mobility — your free foot and the far hip grip allow you to circle around the opponent faster than from side control or mount. Knee-on-belly is a transitional pin, not a resting position.
whyItWorks: Knee pressure on the sternum/solar plexus creates discomfort and breathing restriction that forces the opponent to react
The far hip grip (or collar grip) gives you structural control — you can pull them toward you while driving the knee
The free foot on the mat provides instant mobility — you can transition to mount, side control, north-south, or the back without repositioning
Knee-on-belly is the only pin that does not require full body contact — this makes it ideal for quick transitions
commonMistakes: Letting the opponent trap your foot — once the foot is trapped, you lose mobility and can be swept or reversed
Driving the knee too high (into the throat) or too low (into the hips) — the correct target is the sternum/solar plexus
Staying too long in knee-on-belly without attacking — it is a transitional pin, not a resting position
Leaning too far forward — this compromises your base and allows the opponent to roll you
coachingCues: Knee on the sternum, not the throat
Protect the foot, keep it mobile
Far hip grip controls their movement
safetySummary: Do not drive the knee into the opponent's throat — target the sternum or solar plexus
Knee-on-belly can be painful on the ribs for lighter opponents — be aware of your training partner's comfort level
If the opponent rolls aggressively to escape, release the knee pressure and transition with them rather than resisting

systemLogic.corePrinciple: Knee-on-belly is organized as a transition hub with four branches: Mount → Side Control → North-South → Back Take

decisionTree.action: slide your knee off their belly and step over their near arm to mount. Keep the far hip grip to pull them toward you as you enter mount
drop your knee to the mat beside their hip and slide into side control. Maintain chest-to-chest pressure
walk your knee up their chest toward their head while keeping the far hip grip. Slide to north-south when your knee reaches their chin level
if they turn away or on their side to escape the knee pressure, release the knee, follow their turn, and take the back with a seatbelt
if they stay flat → attack or transition to mount. If they turn away → take the back. If they trap the foot → pummel free and re-establish

moneyDetails: Knee-on-belly scores 2 points in IBJJF — it is the fastest way to score from side control
Knee-on-belly is the most threatening pin to opponents because the immediate discomfort forces them into predictable reactions
Mastering knee-on-belly transitions gives you the most mobile top game in BJJ
fixItFast: If they trap your foot: circle the foot toward your body and re-post it further back
If they are not reacting to the knee pressure: you are in the wrong spot — find the sternum gap and re-position
If they turn away from the pressure: release the knee and take the back immediately
